opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think sparsity has been one of the big, maybe underappreciated, drivers of the inference cost improvements we've seen over the last couple of years. The clearest example is mixture-of-experts. A lot of the frontier models now are MoE, where you might have a very large total parameter count but each token only activates a small fraction of it. Instead of running every token through the entire network, a router picks a few experts. So you get the quality of a much bigger model while paying the compute of a much smaller one per token. That's a really good trade, and the industry has moved toward it pretty decisively.

What's interesting is that the trend has been toward *more* sparsity over time. Early MoE models activated something like two out of eight experts. Now you see models with many more, finer-grained experts, where the ratio of active to total parameters keeps shrinking. People found that if you get the routing and load balancing right, you can push that ratio quite far without losing much quality.

The catch, and this is where my systems hat comes in, is that sparsity is only useful if the hardware and software can actually exploit it. FLOPs per token go down, but memory doesn't go away. You still have to store all those parameters, and during decoding you're often memory-bandwidth bound rather than compute bound. So MoE changes the bottleneck. You have to think about expert parallelism, how you shard experts across GPUs, the all-to-all communication, and batching so each expert sees enough tokens to keep the tensor cores busy. A lot of the engineering work in inference systems over the past year or two has been about making those sparse models run efficiently at scale.

There's also sparsity on the attention side. As context lengths get longer, attending to every previous token gets expensive, especially the KV cache. So there's been a lot of work on sparse or selective attention, where you only attend to the most relevant parts of the context, plus hybrid architectures that mix attention with state-space or linear-attention layers that compress history into a fixed-size state. I see these as related ideas: you don't need to touch every parameter or every token for every prediction, and if you're smart about what to skip, you save a lot.

So my view is that sparsity is one of the main levers, alongside lower precision, better kernels, and things like speculative decoding. And it's a good example of hardware and model co-design. The architectures that win aren't just the ones that look good on paper in FLOP counts; they're the ones that map well onto the hardware we have. I expect we'll keep seeing more sparsity, and the interesting questions will be about making it hardware-friendly rather than whether to use it at all.

r001.rationale: It says newer MoE models use more, finer-grained experts and that the active-to-total parameter ratio keeps shrinking compared with earlier models.

r002.rationale: It discusses per-token compute savings and inference at scale, but does not state that sparsity is especially beneficial when serving large numbers of users.

r003.rationale: It calls sparsity a major inference lever and describes hardware/model co-design, but does not attribute a substantial share of recent inference improvements to co-design between the architecture and inference stack.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so sparsity is a really interesting one, because I think it gets lumped together as one thing when it's actually several different things happening at different layers of the stack.

The most visible form is mixture of experts. If you look at DeepSeek V3, or Llama 4, or what we think the frontier labs are doing, you have a model with, say, six or seven hundred billion total parameters, but each token only touches thirty or forty billion of them. That's a huge win for inference because the dominant cost, at least in the decode phase, is moving weights from HBM to the compute units. If you only have to touch a twentieth of the weights per token, in principle you're doing a twentieth of the memory traffic. In practice it's not that clean, because you need to batch tokens so that each expert gets enough work to actually saturate the GPU, and that pushes you toward expert parallelism across many devices, and then you're paying for all-to-all communication. So a lot of the recent inference improvements are really systems improvements that make MoE sparsity actually realizable on hardware, rather than just theoretical FLOP savings.

The second form is sparsity in attention. The KV cache has become the thing that dominates memory at long context, and once you're memory-bound on the KV cache, you start asking which tokens actually matter. So you see things like DeepSeek's sparse attention, or Native Sparse Attention, or various block-sparse and retrieval-style approaches where each query only attends to a subset of the keys. This is closer to what I spent a lot of time on with FlashAttention: the question is always whether the sparsity pattern is structured enough that you can turn it into fewer memory reads and fewer tile loads, or whether it's just irregular enough that the hardware can't exploit it. Unstructured sparsity is almost useless on GPUs. Block sparsity, where you skip whole tiles, is where you actually get speedups.

And then there's a third thing I'd mention, which is sparsity at the level of what you even compute per step. Speculative decoding, multi-token prediction, these are not sparsity in the classical sense, but they come from the same observation: most of the work the model does per token is kind of redundant, and if you can skip or amortize it, you win.

The way I tie it together is that for the last several years, the hardware has been getting more compute much faster than it's been getting memory bandwidth. So anything that reduces bytes moved per useful output is where the leverage is. Sparsity, in all these forms, is really a bet that you can trade a little bit of model quality, or sometimes none at all, for a lot less memory movement. The algorithmic side of that bet is mostly settled, I think. The hard part now is the systems side: scheduling, load balancing, kernels that are actually efficient when the work is irregular. That's where I think most of the interesting inference engineering is going right now.

r001.rationale: It gives an example of MoE models activating only a fraction of their parameters, but does not say that newer models activate a smaller fraction of experts than earlier models.

r002.rationale: It discusses batching tokens to keep experts busy, but does not state that sparsity is particularly beneficial when serving large numbers of users.

r003.rationale: It attributes many recent inference improvements to systems work that makes MoE sparsity practical on hardware, conveying that architecture and the inference stack work together.

astra-6.text:
I think sparsity is an important part of the story, but I’d distinguish between doing fewer operations and actually making inference faster. Those aren’t always the same thing. GPUs are very good at dense matrix multiplication, so if you introduce sparsity in a way that requires a lot of irregular memory access or coordination, you can lose the benefit of skipping computation.

Mixture-of-experts models are one example where that tradeoff can work well. You have a large number of parameters, but you activate only a subset for each token. That gives you more model capacity without paying the full compute cost every time. But you still have to handle routing, moving tokens between devices, and making sure the experts get enough work to run efficiently.

Sparse attention is another opportunity: can you avoid reading parts of the context that aren’t useful for the current token? Especially with long contexts, that can reduce both computation and memory traffic. The challenge is choosing what to skip without hurting quality.

So I’d think of sparsity as an algorithm and systems problem together. The useful metric isn’t just what fraction of the model is inactive; it’s whether you get lower latency or higher throughput at the quality you need.

r001.rationale: It says MoE models activate a subset of experts per token, but gives no trend toward activating a smaller fraction in newer models than in earlier ones.

r002.rationale: It discusses compute costs and efficiency, but does not say sparsity is particularly beneficial when serving large numbers of users.

r003.rationale: It frames sparsity as an algorithm-and-systems problem, but does not attribute a substantial share of recent inference improvements to co-design between model architecture and the inference stack.

sol-6.1.text:
I think sparsity is an important part of the story, but you have to distinguish theoretical savings from actual speedups. You can have a model that does fewer FLOPs on paper and still doesn’t run faster, because the GPU is spending its time moving data or coordinating irregular computation.

Mixture of experts is a good example. You can increase the total number of parameters while activating only a subset for each token. That gives you more model capacity for a given amount of compute. But now you have routing, communication between devices, and load balancing to deal with. Those costs matter a lot in inference.

There’s a similar opportunity with sparse attention: can we avoid reading and computing over every previous token? The challenge is finding a pattern that preserves quality and maps efficiently to the hardware. Skipping large blocks is generally much easier to turn into a speedup than skipping scattered individual elements.

So I see sparsity as a model-and-systems co-design problem. The question isn’t just how many operations you can remove. It’s whether you can remove work in a way that actually reduces memory traffic and latency on the hardware you’re using.

r001.rationale: It says MoE models activate only a subset of parameters per token, but does not identify a trend toward activating a smaller fraction in newer models than in earlier ones.

r002.rationale: It does not mention serving large numbers of users or say sparsity is especially beneficial at that scale.

r003.rationale: It calls sparsity a model-and-systems co-design problem, but does not attribute a substantial share of recent inference improvements to co-design between architecture and the inference stack.
